title: Race, explain and transfer
target: Evaluate a model against measured performance and defend design decisions.
criteria: Report measured distance, time and average speed.
Compare actual speed with a stated prediction.
Use evidence to explain three physical design choices.

authoring.limitations: Reasoning evidence only. Multiple choice does not certify physical performance. Teacher reviews before assigning and rates mastery separately.

cpa.prompt: In a supplied race example, a car travels 6.3 m in 9.0 s. Which report has the correct average speed and units?
options: 1.43 s/m as speed
cpa.guide: 6.3/9.0 = 0.70 m/s. Average speed uses length per time, not acceleration units.
cpa.freshness: New scenario and/or model data, independently answerable without worksheet answers.

demand.evidence: Apply the physical relationship to new data.

cpa.prompt: Which report separates a real observation from a model prediction?
options: “Our car must match the example because it is the same color.”
“Measured 0.60 m/s,” copied from the model without timing.
“Predicted and measured mean the same thing.”
“Measured time: 8.2 s over 4.1 m; model speed: 0.60 m/s.”
cpa.guide: Measured distance and time are evidence; a predicted speed comes from a model and must be labeled separately.
cpa.freshness: New scenario and/or model data, independently answerable without worksheet answers.

demand.evidence: Select a claim supported by the stated evidence and assumptions.

cpa.prompt: A model predicts 0.80 m/s. Example measured average speed is 0.60 m/s. Relative to the prediction, how much lower is the measured speed?
cpa.guide: Difference = 0.20; 0.20/0.80 × 100 = 25%. Use the stated reference in the denominator.
cpa.freshness: New scenario and/or model data, independently answerable without worksheet answers.

demand.evidence: Apply the physical relationship to new data.

cpa.prompt: Measured speed is below a no-slip, no-loss prediction. Which explanation is appropriately cautious?
options: Rubbing, slip, or lower loaded motor rate could contribute; test these possibilities.
The measurement proves energy was destroyed.
Only the wheel color can explain it.
The model must be exact because it contains numbers.
cpa.guide: Ideal assumptions can omit losses and load effects. A mismatch does not uniquely identify its cause.
cpa.freshness: New scenario and/or model data, independently answerable without worksheet answers.

demand.evidence: Select a claim supported by the stated evidence and assumptions.

cpa.prompt: Which explanation connects three design choices to physics?
options: Larger wheels always win; alignment never matters; current disappears at the motor.
Larger wheels change distance per turn; alignment limits unequal rubbing; secure wiring maintains the intended circuit.
Wheel size, alignment, and wiring only change appearance.
Paint creates power; alignment stores charge; wires provide fuel.
cpa.guide: The correct set connects geometry, forces, and electrical continuity without unconditional performance claims.
cpa.freshness: New scenario and/or model data, independently answerable without worksheet answers.

demand.evidence: Compare evidence and identify a physical relationship.

cpa.prompt: A new race course starts on a steeper ramp. Why might a slower gear reduction be useful even though its ideal top speed is lower?
options: It guarantees greater speed and torque at unchanged power.
It can provide greater axle torque to overcome the required driving load.
It creates energy from the gears.
It removes gravity from the car.
cpa.guide: A reduction trades rotational speed for torque. Whether it improves the race requires testing the new course.
cpa.freshness: New scenario and/or model data, independently answerable without worksheet answers.

demand.evidence: Select a claim supported by the stated evidence and assumptions.
